chunks: Musa ibn al-Qasim from al-Jarimi, from the two of them, from Ibn Muskan, from Abu Basir, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:

I asked him about a person in ihram who killed a pigeon from the pigeons of the Sanctuary (Haram) while being outside the Sanctuary. He said, 'Upon him is a sheep.' I said, 'And if he killed it inside the Sanctuary?' He said, 'Upon him is a sheep and the value of the pigeon.' I said, 'And if he killed it in the Sanctuary while he is in ihram?' He said, 'Upon him is its price, there is no other upon him.' I said, 'And whoever kills a chick from the chicks of the pigeons while he is in ihram?' He said, 'Upon him is a ewe.'

key_terms.حَمَامَةِ الْحَرَمِ: The pigeons of the Sanctuary (specifically Mecca)
key_terms.حَمَلٌ: A young ewe (a specific unit of compensation)
key_terms.شَاةٌ: A sheep (a specific unit of compensation)
key_terms.مُحْرِمٍ: A pilgrim in the state of ihram (ritual consecration)

ai.seo_question: What is the compensation for a pilgrim in ihram who kills a pigeon in the Haram?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* elucidates the graduated financial penalties (kaffarah) for killing sanctuary birds, distinguishing between the sanctity of the location (Haram) and the state of the pilgrim (ihram). It highlights the juristic nuance that while killing inside the Haram while in ihram incurs both the bird's value and a sheep, killing outside the Haram while in ihram requires only a sheep, reflecting the interplay of spatial and ritual sanctity. This ruling underscores the Shia scholarly emphasis on precise attribution of liability based on the convergence of these two factors.
